acceptance.criterion: Live and seed budget caps are enforced before any request leaves the process, and the wall-clock deadline holds against slow servers, including a first body byte at half the budget followed by a stall
acceptance.expected: max_calls, max_input_tokens (one token per serialized request byte), max_cost_per_call_usd and max_elapsed_seconds each stop the run before the offending request; the TTL wait counts against max_elapsed_seconds; every response and socket is closed on every path
acceptance.observed: Exact-byte precharge inside MCPClient._post, a watchdog that shuts the socket down at an absolute deadline, and explicit closing are covered by the preserved hard-cap regression tests, TestWallClockDeadline and TestResponseClosureAndStallDeadline. The cumulative ledger (evals/hosted/lib/ledger.py) makes the four caps hold across seed, retry and live processes: every request is reserved durably before it leaves, a reservation is never refunded, a corrupt, empty, torn, conflicting or missing ledger blocks, and only the explicit --init-ledger step creates one (test_ledger.py, TestCumulativeLedger, TestInitLedgerCommand). The elapsed deadline is rechecked after the durable reservation and passed into the lock wait; a 50 ms reservation delay under a 10 ms cap and a real competing lock held past the cap each send zero requests to a loopback server. The stall case ran 0.61 s against a 0.6 s budget. DNS resolution is not covered by the deadline, so there is no end-to-end time guarantee against a hostname. The ledger is a local guard, not tamper-proof: see limitations. No hosted endpoint was contacted.

The wall-clock deadline does not cover DNS resolution (getaddrinfo cannot be interrupted), so no total end-to-end time guarantee is claimed for a manifest that names a hostname; use literal IPs or already-resolvable hosts. The budget guard charges one token per serialized request byte, an upper bound roughly four times stricter than chars/4.

The seed's elapsed cap must cover the whole run, including a real 65 s wait. Preflight and seed block a cap below TTL + margin + tail (95 s), but that floor is necessary, not sufficient: the cap must also cover seeding the positive account and the calls before the wait.

The local lexical control's empty cases run against isolated brains holding one unrelated filler fact (seedbrain refuses an empty brain) and are scored strictly: returning the filler fails. The production lexical fallback (internal/index.LiteralFTSQuery) implicit-ANDs every query term including stopwords, so natural-language questions almost never lexically match a short fact statement regardless of the corpus's designed word-overlap category. See embedding-eval.md 'Known limits'.

The local-service run has its own label, evidence_level local-process. This result stays at evidence_level fixture because no provider or semantic measurement exists; that run does not raise it. It ran the serenity binary hashed above (d738c024...) on loopback with SERENITY_HOSTED_DEV=1 in an owned directory under /tmp, and its report records the exact source commit (dcf3174, clean harness tree), zero auth failures, the redaction check and the confirmed-gone owned PID.

Fixture versus live-provider evidence: a loopback, private-range or localhost endpoint, or an environment.kind of local-fixture, always yields evidence_level fixture and a status no higher than PARTIAL, and the Hit@5 row is NOT_RUN or FAIL, never PASS. Host names are not resolved, so a name pointed at a local address is not detected as local. Even a remote endpoint does not prove the provider: provider.declared records the manifest's pin, provider.observed lists only the endpoints called with provider_identity_verified false, and provider.qualification_prerequisites lists what a real run must still show.

The cumulative ledger is a local guard against accidental overspend, not a defence against its owner. A hash chain cannot detect removal of a whole suffix back to a previously valid prefix, or an edit of the final record, and the owner can delete, rewrite or restore the files. Existing empty, corrupt or torn files block; a missing ledger blocks; renewing an allowance is an intentional offline step (--init-ledger with a new authorization), never automatic. The guarantee that holds is narrower: within the files as written, no process can spend past the four bound caps.

The deadline controls only this process's monotonic clock, the lock wait and the socket. It does not control wall-clock jumps, DNS resolution or anything the server does after the request leaves. A reservation that expires between the durable write and the send is retained, counted as reserved_not_sent, and never refunded.

The gateway allows 120 requests per minute per account (fixed one-minute window; 429 with Retry-After: 60) and the harness does not pace itself. The local run waited between phases to stay inside the limit. A real run should pace requests or leave at least 60 s between phases; no pacing or 429 handling was added to the harness.

The service's remember tool silently ignores unknown arguments (the expiry argument is ttl, an absolute ISO instant). The harness guards against that by requiring the service to echo valid_until before it trusts a TTL. The harness's MCP handshake was wrong for the real transport (session id, MCP-Protocol-Version and notifications/initialized are required); it is fixed and tested.

One local-service attempt failed intermittently with an OSError while the owned directory was being removed, on a disk about 93 percent full. Cleanup now retries, re-checks that the directory is still the owned one, and reports a leftover instead of hiding it. Later runs, including the recorded one, left nothing behind.
